title: Second Judge Blocks $100,000 H-1B Fee, Including Its One-Year Extension
excerpt: A California federal judge has barred agencies from enforcing the $100,000 payment on new H-1B petitions, ruling that the administration skipped required rulemaking — the second court order blocking a fee the president extended for another year in September.
body:
• A federal judge in Oakland ruled on September 30 that agencies may not enforce the $100,000 payment on new H-1B petitions, because the policy was imposed without the public notice-and-comment rulemaking the Administrative Procedure Act requires.
  • The order covers both the original September 2025 proclamation and the September 18, 2026 extension that renewed the fee for another year past its September 21 expiry.
  • It is the second block on the fee: a Massachusetts judge vacated it in June in a case brought by 20 states, and an appeals court refused in July to reinstate it.
  • For employers and workers, the practical position today is that the $100,000 payment is not being collected on new petitions while the orders stand — but the Department of Homeland Security is pursuing a formal rule that would set a similar fee of about $103,000.

A second federal judge has blocked the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, ruling that the agencies charged with collecting it never followed the rulemaking process federal law requires. US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, ruled on September 30 in Global Nurse Force v. Trump that US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department failed to follow necessary rule-making processes before implementing the fee, according to Reuters.

Judge Gilliam granted a request by a coalition of unions, employers and nonprofits to stop the agencies enforcing the payment while the lawsuit proceeds. The plaintiffs' counsel at the Justice Action Center say the order bars any agency action to implement or enforce the payment under either the original 2025 proclamation or its 2026 extension, until the government completes notice-and-comment rulemaking. The court also denied the government's motion to dismiss the case.

"Today's decision protects a system that was thrown into chaos overnight."

— Steve Bressler, Democracy Forward, representing the plaintiffs

A fee extended, then blocked again

The $100,000 payment was imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025 and was originally set to expire on September 21, 2026. President Trump recently extended it for another year, Reuters reported. That extension is what makes the California ruling significant: it does not merely block a lapsing policy, it blocks the renewed one as well.

The ruling is the second court order against the fee. In June, a federal judge in Boston temporarily blocked it in a separate case brought by 20 states, and a Boston-based appeals court in July declined to pause that decision. The legal theories differ by case. The California case turns on administrative procedure — whether agencies could turn a proclamation into a working fee regime through memos and guidance alone. Other challenges argue the president has no authority to set such a fee at all, a question the California court did not decide. One court has gone the other way: the US Chamber of Commerce, the country's largest business lobbying group, filed a third lawsuit, and is appealing a judge's decision rejecting its claims that Trump had no authority to set the fee.

The parallel track: a permanent fee through rulemaking

Even as the proclamation-based fee stalls in court, the administration is building a version designed to survive procedural challenge. The Department of Homeland Security in August moved to adopt a permanent fee of about $103,000 through formal rulemaking. When finalized, that rule will likely be challenged in court too, Reuters noted, but on different legal issues than the lawsuits over the fee set by proclamation. Employers can track the underlying programme rules on the USCIS H-1B specialty occupations page.

What this means for Indian professionals

Indian nationals account for roughly seven in ten approved H-1B petitions, so no group has more riding on the outcome. For now, the two blocking orders mean the $100,000 payment is not a live cost on a new petition. The risk has not disappeared; it has changed shape. If the DHS rule is finalized at about $103,000, the fee could return through a channel the courts have not yet ruled on, and the appeals in the existing cases could still revive the proclamation version. Employers planning 2027 hiring should budget for both possibilities rather than assume the fee is gone for good.

What happens next

The California case continues, with a joint case statement due October 20 and a case management conference on October 27. The government's appeals in the state-led case remain pending, and the Chamber of Commerce appeal is proceeding separately. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the California ruling, according to Reuters.
